abstract: Common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus) have a high rate of twinning during pregnancy and exhibit an unusual phenomenon whereby stem cells migrate between fetuses in utero. These cells are integrated into a growing sibling resulting in each individual being a chimera of self and sibling. We mapped the distribution of chimerism across 145 marmosets by amplicon sequencing, showing high levels of chimerism in lateral mesoderm-derived tissues. By integrating pedigree and clinical records with estimates of chimerism we identified litter size to be a major determinant of chimerism and lifespan and demonstrate that chimerism and litter size are both heritable traits. Using exome sequencing of ~400 marmosets we identified major loci associated with variation in litter size and chimerism. These findings have implications for our understanding of self- and non-self across evolutionary biology, immunity and medicine.
